Hercule Poirot. The legendary Belgian detective created by Agatha Christie, appearing in thirty-nine novels and numerous short stories over nearly fifty years. With his trademark fastidious manners, magnificent mustache, and unwavering faith in his "little grey cells," Poirot became one of detective fiction's most recognizable figures. Unlike the physically active sleuths of earlier tradition, Poirot solves murders through psychological insight and logical deduction, often remaining sedentary while reconstructing the criminal's mental state. He represents the triumph of intellect over physical prowess and the power of understanding human nature.

Poirot is fastidiously Belgian, not French—a point he insists upon. He is small, dapper, and neurotic about order and cleanliness, and these eccentricities are integral to his character and his detective method. His method relies on psychology and the psychology of human nature. He reconstructs crime not by examining physical evidence but by understanding the emotional dynamics among suspects. This psychological approach to detection was revolutionary.

Murder on the Orient Express, published in nineteen thirty-four, is his most famous case. A murdered man is discovered with twelve suspects trapped on a snowbound train. Poirot deduces that all are guilty of a conspiracy born from justice. And Then There Were None, published in nineteen thirty-nine, features no recurring detective but is Christie's masterpiece and arguably the greatest puzzle-mystery ever written. Ten strangers are lured to an island, accused of past murders, and systematically killed according to a nursery rhyme.

Poirot's catchphrase invokes his "little grey cells," emphasizing the intellectual nature of his detection. He deprecates physical investigation in favor of understanding motive, psychology, and human contradiction. He ages throughout the novels, written over decades, and Christie eventually depicted his death in Curtain, written in nineteen forty but published in nineteen seventy-five, granting her creation a definitive ending.

Poirot is Christie's most famous contribution to detective fiction. He is central to the genre's history and represents the intellectual detective tradition. Sherlock Holmes is his predecessor and archetype. Both share the conviction that logic and psychology solve crime, though Poirot emphasizes emotion where Holmes prioritizes reason. Mystery is the core of Poirot's narrative function. Each Poirot story is an intricate puzzle for reader and detective alike. Murder on the Orient Express is his most celebrated case and a model of plot construction. Psychology is Poirot's method. He is a psychologist of crime as much as a detective, understanding the human heart as the key to criminal behavior.
